summary: Defines a MIB with the elements common to monitoring any network service application, including a table of monitorable applications, counts of associations to each, and basic status information. It was replaced by RFC 2248.

eli5.summary: A dashboard that shows which services are running and how many people are connected to each one.

subtitle: A common MIB for monitoring network service applications.

tldr.problem: As networks grew more complex, administrators needed to monitor the applications providing network services. Existing tools focused on lower layers and could not see what was happening at the application level.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1565 defines a reusable MIB module with objects common to any network service: a table of running applications, counts of inbound and outbound connections, status information, and details about active associations.
tldr.outcome: It was replaced by RFC 2248, which refined the same concepts. This MIB serves as a building block for application-specific MIBs for services like mail (MTA) and directory services (DSA).

today: RFC 1565 was obsoleted by RFC 2248. The concept of a common application MIB remains valid and is still used as a foundation for application-specific monitoring.

sections.title: The Need for Application Monitoring
sections.content:
RFC 1565 addresses the challenge of managing networked applications. The traditional approach of monitoring routers and network infrastructure does not reveal whether application services are healthy and responsive. A mail server or directory service might be running, but neither its throughput nor user load can be seen from the network layer.

The MIB defined here applies to both TCP/IP and OSI applications, and it is designed to be simple enough that any network service can use it, yet extensible so that service-specific MIBs can add their own objects.
sections.eli5: Managers need to see if important services like mail or directory are running. A simple way to check on them is needed.

sections.title: Application Objects and Associations
sections.content:
The MIB defines two main tables. The application table (applTable) lists every network service running on a system, indexed by an integer. For each application, the MIB records its name, version, when it started, its current operational status (up, down, halted, congested, restarting), and counters for both inbound and outbound associations.

The association table (assocTable) tracks individual connections. Each association records the remote application identifier, the protocol being used, whether the remote end is a client or peer, and how long the association has been active. This allows administrators to see not just that a service is running, but also to understand the load and patterns of use.
sections.eli5: One table lists the services and how busy they are. Another table lists each connection to a service, showing who is calling and when.

sections.title: Counters and Status Information
sections.content:
For each application, the MIB tracks four categories of information. Basic status includes the application name, version, startup time, and operational state. Active connections are counted separately for inbound (responder) and outbound (initiator) associations. Cumulative statistics count the total number of inbound and outbound associations since startup. Activity timestamps record when the application last had inbound and outbound activity, helping to detect stalled or dormant services.

Additionally, counters track rejected inbound associations and failed outbound associations, giving administrators insight into connection problems or capacity issues.
sections.eli5: For each service, you get numbers: how many people are connected now, how many have connected in total, and when someone last used it.

sections.title: Scope and Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
RFC 1565 deliberately keeps scope narrow. It does not provide facilities to manage the host itself (that is the Host Resources MIB), nor to configure or control the application (that would require authentication and is left to application-specific MIBs). The RFC focuses purely on transient, observable aspects: is the service running, how many connections does it have, is it under strain.

Static configuration information is expected to come from directory services, not this MIB. The design links the SNMP-managed object to a directory entry by storing the Distinguished Name, so that detailed configuration and policy information can be looked up separately.
sections.eli5: This MIB shows what is happening right now. Configuration and policy live elsewhere.

sections.title: The MIB Definition
sections.content: The MIB module is named APPLICATION-MIB and is defined using SNMPv2 conventions (RFC 1442, RFC 1448). It assigns the MIB subtree { mib-2 27 }. Two groups are defined: the basic applGroup, which contains the 13 mandatory objects for application monitoring, and the optional assocGroup, which adds 4 objects for association-level monitoring. Two compliance levels are specified: basic compliance supports applGroup alone; full compliance requires both groups.
sections.eli5: The MIB uses SNMP version 2 format and defines two sets of objects: one for basic service status, and one (optional) for detailed connection tracking.
